Decomposing differences in life expectancy

Source: vignettes/decomposition.Rmd
decomposition.Rmd

A difference in life expectancy, between deprivation quintiles, between two years or between two forecasts, is the sum of differences in death rates at many ages and from many causes. A decomposition attributes it to those ages and causes, and, for populations made of subgroups, separates the effect of the subgroups’ mortality from the effect of their composition. In mortensor this is a post-processing step, mt_decompose(), that works on observed data, on forecast draws, and on both together. Forecasts are decomposed draw by draw, so every contribution has an interval.

Method Decomposes Reference
"arriaga" (default for life expectancy) life expectancy, by age (and cause) Arriaga (1984), symmetric form as in Riffe et al. (2024)
"horiuchi" any function of the rates Horiuchi, Wilmoth and Pletcher (2008)
"stepwise" any function of the rates Andreev, Shkolnikov and Begun (2002)
"kitagawa" crude death rate: rates and age structure Kitagawa (1955)
groups with composition = "radix" life expectancy of a population of subgroups fixed from the start (sex, education): subgroup rates and composition Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós (2024), “Arriaga meets Kitagawa”
groups with composition = "pooled" life expectancy of the pooled rates (areas, regions): subgroup rates and age-specific composition parametrisation specific to this package (reference unknown); line integral of Horiuchi et al. (2008) 
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")

The data are the ONS deaths and populations of England by sex, 5-year age group and IMD quintile, 2001-2019 (ons_data; Source: Office for National Statistics licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0). Q1 is the most deprived quintile.

The deprivation gap by age

Each quintile compared with Q1 in 2019, with 200 Poisson draws of the deaths for the intervals:

gap <- mt_decompose(x, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = 2019, n_draws = 200)
gap
#> <mt_decomposition> life expectancy at 0, method arriaga; 8 comparison(s), means over 200 draws
#>    comparison    sex   from     to period from_value to_value difference
#>         <int> <char> <char> <char>  <num>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1 female     Q1     Q2   2019     79.825   82.501      2.676
#> 2:          2 female     Q1     Q3   2019     79.825   83.929      4.103
#> 3:          3 female     Q1     Q4   2019     79.825   85.020      5.195
#> 4:          4 female     Q1     Q5   2019     79.825   86.289      6.464
#> 5:          5   male     Q1     Q2   2019     75.429   78.596      3.167
#> 6:          6   male     Q1     Q3   2019     75.429   80.604      5.175
#> 7:          7   male     Q1     Q4   2019     75.429   81.818      6.389
#> 8:          8   male     Q1     Q5   2019     75.429   83.094      7.664
#>    difference_q0.025 difference_q0.5 difference_q0.975 sum_contributions
#>                <num>           <num>             <num>             <num>
#> 1:             2.515           2.682             2.826             2.676
#> 2:             3.964           4.109             4.249             4.103
#> 3:             5.027           5.198             5.335             5.195
#> 4:             6.318           6.466             6.615             6.464
#> 5:             3.001           3.166             3.332             3.167
#> 6:             5.013           5.168             5.312             5.175
#> 7:             6.223           6.383             6.564             6.389
#> 8:             7.517           7.657             7.831             7.664
#>    max_residual
#>           <num>
#> 1:      1.3e-14
#> 2:      1.7e-14
#> 3:      1.5e-14
#> 4:      1.6e-14
#> 5:      1.6e-14
#> 6:      1.5e-14
#> 7:      1.6e-14
#> 8:      1.4e-14

The totals list one comparison per row: the life expectancy of the reference (from_value) and of the level (to_value), their difference with its interval, and the sum of the age contributions, which equals the difference (max_residual is the largest discrepancy over draws). Values are means over the draws; quantiles are in the columns difference_q* and in summary(). summary(gap, by = "age") gives the contributions; the plot shows them for the gap between Q5 and Q1:

mt_plot_decomposition(gap, by = "age", comparisons = list(to = "Q5"))

s <- summary(gap, by = "age")[to == "Q5"]
s[, band := cut(as.numeric(sub("[-+].*", "", age)), c(-1, 39, 64, 84, Inf),
                labels = c("0-39", "40-64", "65-84", "85+"))]
dcast(s[, .(contribution = round(sum(mean), 2)), by = .(sex, band)], sex ~ band, value.var = "contribution")
#> Key: <sex>
#>       sex  0-39 40-64 65-84   85+
#>    <char> <num> <num> <num> <num>
#> 1: female  0.55  2.01  3.20  0.70
#> 2:   male  0.93  3.01  3.29  0.43

The gap of 6.5 years for women and 7.7 years for men comes mostly from ages 40 to 84 (5.2 and 6.3 years): deaths at working ages and in early old age are much more frequent in Q1. Ages below 40 add 0.6 years for women and 0.9 years for men; infant mortality alone adds 0.2 years for women. With Poisson draws of the observed deaths, the intervals of single ages are narrow.

The methods agree closely. Symmetric Arriaga and symmetric stepwise replacement are identical for life expectancy, because Arriaga’s decomposition is stepwise replacement from the oldest to the youngest age; the line integral assigns interactions between ages slightly differently:

meth <- rbindlist(lapply(c("arriaga", "horiuchi", "stepwise"), function(m) {
  d <- mt_decompose(x, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = 2019, method = m)
  summary(d, by = "age")[to == "Q5" & sex == "female", .(age, method = m, mean = round(mean, 3))]
}))
meth[, age := factor(age, unique(age))]
dcast(meth, age ~ method, value.var = "mean")[age %in% c("0", "40-44", "60-64", "75-79", "90+")]
#> Key: <age>
#>       age arriaga horiuchi stepwise
#>    <fctr>   <num>    <num>    <num>
#> 1:      0   0.221    0.221    0.221
#> 2:  40-44   0.232    0.231    0.232
#> 3:  60-64   0.651    0.650    0.651
#> 4:  75-79   0.881    0.886    0.881
#> 5:    90+   0.276    0.272    0.276

Causes behind the gap

Causes of death are a stratum variable whose rates add up to all causes. cause names it. The total level ("all") is left out because mt_group_levels(total = "all") records it in the data; without such a record (or a hierarchy), mt_decompose() stops rather than count all causes as one more cause. At ages 50 and over (as in “Inequality in England”):

causes <- names(ons_data)[-(1:7)]
xc <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile", "cause"),
              age = "age_group", value = list(deaths = c(all = "all_causes", causes), population = "population"))
xc <- mt_as_exposure(xc, type = "midyear")
xc <- mt_subset(xc, ages = c(50, Inf), periods = c(2019, 2019))
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "cause", ons_cause_groups, other = "rest", total = "all", additive = "rates")
gc <- mt_decompose(xc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", cause = "cause")
sc <- summary(gc, by = "cause")[to == "Q5"]
dcast(sc, cause ~ sex, value.var = "mean")[order(-female), lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v, 2) else v)]
#>                 cause female  male
#>                <char>  <num> <num>
#>  1:              rest   1.37  1.42
#>  2:       respiratory   0.89  0.77
#>  3:       lung_cancer   0.71  0.71
#>  4:               ihd   0.65  1.09
#>  5:     other_cancers   0.54  0.65
#>  6:          dementia   0.52  0.34
#>  7:     liver_alcohol   0.28  0.51
#>  8:            stroke   0.21  0.21
#>  9: other_circulatory   0.18  0.17
#> 10:          diabetes   0.12  0.12
#> 11: colorectal_cancer   0.04  0.09
#> 12:   breast_prostate   0.04  0.07
mt_plot_decomposition(gc, by = "age", fill = "cause", comparisons = list(to = "Q5"))

Each age contribution is split over the causes in proportion to their rate differences (Riffe et al. 2024, eqs. 12-13). Of the gap in life expectancy at 50, chronic lower respiratory diseases, lung cancer and ischaemic heart disease contribute most among the named causes, for both sexes, and the remaining causes together (rest) contribute a large share. Causes with higher rates in Q5 than in Q1 would have negative contributions.

Change over time and the composition of England

The life expectancy of a population of subgroups changes because the mortality of every subgroup changes and because the population shifts between subgroups. groups names the subgroups, and composition decides which life expectancy of the whole population is decomposed. The choice matters, so it has no default.

Subgroups fixed from the start of life: composition = "radix". Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós (2024) treat the life expectancy of a population as the mean of the subgroups’ life expectancies, weighted by their shares at the starting age, as if subgroup life tables were blended at the radix. A Kitagawa decomposition of that mean separates the composition from the change within each subgroup, which is then split by age. The authors state the condition: membership must be fixed from the starting age on, and later shares must change through mortality only, as for sex, education from age 30 or country of birth. Sex is such a subgroup: the life expectancy at birth of both sexes in each quintile, with the sex ratio at birth as the composition:

both <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "sex", composition = "radix")
both
#> <mt_decomposition> life expectancy at 0, method arriaga, radix composition; 5 comparison(s), 1 draw
#> Values: means of the subgroups' values weighted by their shares at age 0 (subgroups blended at the radix),
#> not the values of the pooled rates.
#>    comparison quintile   from     to from_value to_value difference
#>         <int>   <char> <char> <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1       Q1   2001   2019     74.598   77.572      2.974
#> 2:          2       Q2   2001   2019     77.149   80.503      3.354
#> 3:          3       Q3   2001   2019     78.835   82.218      3.383
#> 4:          4       Q4   2001   2019     79.860   83.374      3.514
#> 5:          5       Q5   2001   2019     80.995   84.643      3.647
#>    sum_contributions max_residual
#>                <num>        <num>
#> 1:             2.974      1.8e-15
#> 2:             3.354      8.4e-15
#> 3:             3.383      1.4e-14
#> 4:             3.514      4.4e-15
#> 5:             3.647      8.0e-15
summary(both, by = c("component", "group"))[, .(quintile, component, group, mean = round(mean, 3))]
#>     quintile   component  group   mean
#>       <char>      <char> <char>  <num>
#>  1:       Q1        rate female  1.060
#>  2:       Q1        rate   male  1.942
#>  3:       Q1 composition   <NA> -0.028
#>  4:       Q2        rate female  1.374
#>  5:       Q2        rate   male  1.983
#>  6:       Q2 composition   <NA> -0.003
#>  7:       Q3        rate female  1.409
#>  8:       Q3        rate   male  1.988
#>  9:       Q3 composition   <NA> -0.014
#> 10:       Q4        rate female  1.479
#> 11:       Q4        rate   male  2.038
#> 12:       Q4 composition   <NA> -0.004
#> 13:       Q5        rate female  1.686
#> 14:       Q5        rate   male  1.978
#> 15:       Q5 composition   <NA> -0.017

The printout states what the values are: means of women’s and men’s life expectancy weighted by the sex ratio at birth, not the life expectancy of the pooled rates. In every quintile men contributed more to the rise than women (in Q1 1.9 against 1.1 years); the sex ratio at birth hardly changed, so its composition effect is a few hundredths of a year.

Areas and other changing groups: composition = "pooled". Deprivation quintiles are areas: people move between them, and areas change quintile with each IMD version. The condition of the radix version does not hold. The pooled version decomposes the life expectancy of the pooled rates of England (the quintiles weighted by their population at each age, as in published life tables; “current rates” in Vaupel’s terms, while the radix version of Riffe et al. describes “current conditions”). The rates of every quintile and age and the shares at every age are the parameters of a line-integral decomposition (Horiuchi et al. 2008). This parametrisation is specific to this package (reference unknown); others would split the difference differently between rates and composition:

eng <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "quintile", composition = "pooled")
eng
#> <mt_decomposition> life expectancy at 0, method horiuchi, pooled composition; 2 comparison(s), 1 draw
#> Values: of the pooled rates (subgroups weighted by their shares at each age). Pooled composition:
#> a parametrisation specific to this package (reference unknown), decomposed with the line
#> integral of Horiuchi et al. (2008) or stepwise replacement.
#>    comparison    sex   from     to from_value to_value difference
#>         <int> <char> <char> <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1 female   2001   2019     80.649   83.631      2.982
#> 2:          2   male   2001   2019     76.030   79.981      3.951
#>    sum_contributions max_residual
#>                <num>        <num>
#> 1:             2.982      3.6e-05
#> 2:             3.951      7.4e-05
summary(eng, by = c("component", "group"))[, .(sex, component, group, mean = round(mean, 3))]
#>        sex   component  group  mean
#>     <char>      <char> <char> <num>
#>  1: female        rate     Q1 0.462
#>  2: female        rate     Q2 0.568
#>  3: female        rate     Q3 0.601
#>  4: female        rate     Q4 0.615
#>  5: female        rate     Q5 0.635
#>  6: female composition   <NA> 0.101
#>  7:   male        rate     Q1 0.854
#>  8:   male        rate     Q2 0.799
#>  9:   male        rate     Q3 0.785
#> 10:   male        rate     Q4 0.783
#> 11:   male        rate     Q5 0.696
#> 12:   male composition   <NA> 0.033

Life expectancy at birth of England rose by 3.0 years for women and 4.0 years for men. Every quintile contributed about half a year or more; for men, Q1 contributed most. The composition effect is positive and small (0.10 and 0.03 years). Applied to the quintiles, the radix version would give a negative composition effect, because the shares at birth and at older ages moved in opposite directions:

eng_radix <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "quintile", composition = "radix")
rbind(summary(eng, by = "component")[, .(composition = "pooled", sex, component, mean = round(mean, 3))],
      summary(eng_radix, by = "component")[, .(composition = "radix", sex, component, mean = round(mean, 3))])
#>    composition    sex   component   mean
#>         <char> <char>      <char>  <num>
#> 1:      pooled female        rate  2.881
#> 2:      pooled female composition  0.101
#> 3:      pooled   male        rate  3.917
#> 4:      pooled   male composition  0.033
#> 5:       radix female        rate  2.817
#> 6:       radix female composition -0.096
#> 7:       radix   male        rate  3.870
#> 8:       radix   male composition -0.128
E <- mt_array(x, "exposure")
women <- x$strata$label[x$strata$sex == "female"]
round(rbind(birth_2001 = E["0", "2001", women], birth_2019 = E["0", "2019", women],
            age75_2001 = E["75-79", "2001", women], age75_2019 = E["75-79", "2019", women]) /
        rep(c(sum(E["0", "2001", women]), sum(E["0", "2019", women]), sum(E["75-79", "2001", women]),
              sum(E["75-79", "2019", women])), 5), 3)
#>            female.Q1 female.Q2 female.Q3 female.Q4 female.Q5
#> birth_2001     0.249     0.204     0.184     0.178     0.184
#> birth_2019     0.252     0.223     0.195     0.175     0.156
#> age75_2001     0.188     0.200     0.211     0.208     0.193
#> age75_2019     0.143     0.175     0.211     0.232     0.239

At birth the share of Q5 fell (from 18% to 16% for girls), while at ages 75-79, where many deaths occur, it rose from 19% to 24% and the share of Q1 fell from 19% to 14%. The radix version treats the shares at birth as the composition of the whole population, which is wrong for areas. The composition effect is a single number (radix) or one per age (pooled): the separate composition terms of the subgroups are not identified.

Forecasts

Li-Lee forecasts to 2035, decomposed draw by draw. With draws, periods can combine an observed year (held in the draws) with forecast years:

fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), x), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
change <- mt_decompose(fc, periods = c(2019, 2035))
summary(change, by = NULL)[, .(sex, quintile, from_value, to_value, difference, jump_off)]
#>        sex quintile from_value to_value difference    jump_off
#>     <char>   <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>       <num>
#>  1: female       Q1   79.83321 83.38002   3.546810  0.42834663
#>  2: female       Q2   82.49875 85.19000   2.691251  0.24430512
#>  3: female       Q3   83.93153 86.29470   2.363171  0.08339506
#>  4: female       Q4   85.01728 87.04342   2.026131 -0.13923362
#>  5: female       Q5   86.29508 87.95801   1.662930 -0.34119674
#>  6:   male       Q1   75.43067 79.56163   4.130958  0.41338747
#>  7:   male       Q2   78.59779 82.07083   3.473034  0.14018639
#>  8:   male       Q3   80.60501 83.66165   3.056633 -0.04412830
#>  9:   male       Q4   81.82001 84.69466   2.874653 -0.06719945
#> 10:   male       Q5   83.08997 85.79980   2.709830 -0.07113273

A change from an observed to a forecast year contains the step from the observed rates of 2019 to the model’s fitted rates of 2019 (the jump-off, see mt_jump_off()), and with it the noise of the observed year. Column jump_off gives its share: of the forecast gain of 3.5 years for women in Q1, 0.4 years come from this step. observed = "fitted" decomposes the model’s change alone:

change_fit <- mt_decompose(fc, periods = c(2019, 2035), observed = "fitted")
summary(change_fit, by = NULL)[, .(sex, quintile, from_value, to_value, difference, difference_q0.025,
                                   difference_q0.975)]
#>        sex quintile from_value to_value difference difference_q0.025
#>     <char>   <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>             <num>
#>  1: female       Q1   80.26155 83.38002   3.118463        -0.9029978
#>  2: female       Q2   82.74305 85.19000   2.446946        -1.1600297
#>  3: female       Q3   84.01493 86.29470   2.279776        -1.0828860
#>  4: female       Q4   84.87805 87.04342   2.165365        -1.0599289
#>  5: female       Q5   85.95388 87.95801   2.004127        -1.0005026
#>  6:   male       Q1   75.84405 79.56163   3.717571         1.5582410
#>  7:   male       Q2   78.73798 82.07083   3.332848         1.4124004
#>  8:   male       Q3   80.56089 83.66165   3.100761         1.3525203
#>  9:   male       Q4   81.75281 84.69466   2.941852         1.2555216
#> 10:   male       Q5   83.01884 85.79980   2.780963         1.1909061
#>     difference_q0.975
#>                 <num>
#>  1:          6.627991
#>  2:          5.589562
#>  3:          5.175859
#>  4:          4.898247
#>  5:          4.627423
#>  6:          5.960220
#>  7:          5.302733
#>  8:          4.892532
#>  9:          4.669059
#> 10:          4.396472
mt_plot_decomposition(change_fit, by = "age", comparisons = list(quintile = "Q1"))

The model’s gain for women in Q1 (3.1 years) comes mostly from ages 50 to 84. The bars give the mean contribution and the lines the 95% interval of each age over the draws. The intervals are wide and include zero at most ages: the common trend of Li-Lee is uncertain 16 years ahead, and it moves all ages together, so the uncertainty of the ages adds up in the total. observed = "poisson" would add the sampling uncertainty of the observed year.

The gap between Q5 and Q1 in 2019 and in 2035, and its change. For the change, summary(change = ) subtracts the two decompositions draw by draw:

g <- mt_decompose(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = c(2019, 2035))
summary(g, by = NULL)[to == "Q5", .(sex, period, difference, difference_q0.025, difference_q0.975, jump_off)]
#>       sex period difference difference_q0.025 difference_q0.975  jump_off
#>    <char>  <num>      <num>             <num>             <num>     <num>
#> 1: female   2019   6.461871          6.461871          6.461871 0.7695434
#> 2: female   2035   4.577992          3.649408          5.662527        NA
#> 3:   male   2019   7.659303          7.659303          7.659303 0.4845202
#> 4:   male   2035   6.238175          5.633736          6.807403        NA
g_fit <- mt_decompose(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = c(2019, 2035), observed = "fitted")
summary(g_fit, by = NULL, change = c(2019, 2035))[to == "Q5", .(sex, period, from_value, to_value, difference,
                                                                difference_q0.025, difference_q0.975)]
#>       sex       period from_value to_value difference difference_q0.025
#>    <char>       <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>             <num>
#> 1: female 2019 to 2035   5.692328 4.577992 -1.1143361         -2.042920
#> 2:   male 2019 to 2035   7.174783 6.238175 -0.9366078         -1.541046
#>    difference_q0.975
#>                <num>
#> 1:       -0.02980065
#> 2:       -0.36737929

Li-Lee forecasts a female gap of 4.6 years in 2035, against 6.5 observed in 2019. Of this narrowing of 1.9 years, 0.8 years is the jump-off: the Li-Lee fit of 2019 already puts the gap at 5.7 years. The model’s own narrowing, from the fitted 2019 gap, is 1.1 years (95% interval 0.03 to 2.0): the deviations of Q1 from the common trend return towards their average. The vignette “Inequality in England” shows that in 2010-2019 the gap did not behave like this, and that Li-Lee forecast it poorly. anchored() starts the forecast from the observed rates of 2019 and keeps this offset in every forecast year (Lee and Miller 2001); the gap then narrows only by the model’s own change.

Two forecasts of the same year are compared by giving the second as y. Their draws are independent, so they are shuffled before they are paired (pairing = "independent"). Lee-Carter per quintile against Li-Lee, for 2035:

fl <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
mm <- mt_decompose(fc, fl, periods = 2035)
summary(mm, by = NULL)[sex == "female", .(quintile, from_value, to_value, difference, difference_q0.025,
                                          difference_q0.975)]
#>    quintile from_value to_value difference difference_q0.025 difference_q0.975
#>      <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>             <num>             <num>
#> 1:       Q1   83.38002 81.45818 -1.9218316         -6.649883          2.623245
#> 2:       Q2   85.19000 84.66799 -0.5220072         -4.504384          4.044343
#> 3:       Q3   86.29470 86.20373 -0.0909772         -3.992022          4.002413
#> 4:       Q4   87.04342 87.46871  0.4252962         -3.547072          4.280894
#> 5:       Q5   87.95801 89.20283  1.2448255         -2.182106          4.895994
mt_plot_decomposition(mm, by = "age", comparisons = list(quintile = "Q1"))

For women in Q1, Lee-Carter forecasts 1.9 years less than Li-Lee, 1.7 years of it at ages 60 and over: Lee-Carter extrapolates the slower improvement of Q1 at these ages in 2001-2019, while Li-Lee lets Q1 return towards the common trend of all quintiles. The interval of the difference is wide because both forecasts are uncertain; it says how different two independent forecasts can be, not how different the models are.

Other quantities

quantity selects the summary. The probability of dying between 30 and 75 and the age-standardised rate are decomposed by age with the line integral; any function of the rates can be given as well:

pd <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), quantity = "prob_dying", at = 30, to = 75)
summary(pd, by = NULL)[sex == "male", .(quintile, from_value, to_value, difference)]
#>    quintile from_value  to_value  difference
#>      <char>      <num>     <num>       <num>
#> 1:       Q1  0.4928583 0.3893294 -0.10352894
#> 2:       Q2  0.4081154 0.2966236 -0.11149177
#> 3:       Q3  0.3401629 0.2389755 -0.10118739
#> 4:       Q4  0.3045689 0.2098098 -0.09475918
#> 5:       Q5  0.2653566 0.1775151 -0.08784144

The crude death rate changes with the rates and with the age structure of the population. Kitagawa’s decomposition separates the two:

cr <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), quantity = "crude_rate")
dcast(summary(cr, by = "component"), sex + quintile ~ component, value.var = "mean")[
  , lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v) else v)]
#> Key: <sex, quintile>
#>        sex quintile composition  rate
#>     <char>   <char>       <num> <num>
#>  1: female       Q1         -56  -138
#>  2: female       Q2         -23  -214
#>  3: female       Q3          69  -270
#>  4: female       Q4         155  -279
#>  5: female       Q5         262  -301
#>  6:   male       Q1          97  -287
#>  7:   male       Q2         141  -314
#>  8:   male       Q3         240  -350
#>  9:   male       Q4         319  -357
#> 10:   male       Q5         399  -340

Per 100,000, falling rates lowered the crude death rate of every quintile by 140 to 360 deaths. Ageing raised it, most in the least deprived quintiles, whose populations are oldest; only for women in Q1 and Q2 did the age structure lower it. For men in Q5 the crude rate rose although the rates fell.

Choosing a method

  • Life expectancy by age and cause: "arriaga" (exact and fast). Other quantities: "horiuchi" or "stepwise"; the line integral distributes interactions evenly, stepwise replacement depends on the order of the ages.
  • Populations of subgroups: composition = "radix" (Riffe et al.) for subgroups fixed from the starting age (sex, education from 30 or 35, country of birth); "pooled" (a parametrisation specific to this package) for areas, regions and other groups between which people move, and whenever the target is the life expectancy of the whole population as published.
  • Forecasts from an observed year: report the jump-off (jump_off) or decompose from the fitted rates (observed = "fitted"); compare two models with independent draws (the default).
  • Forecasts: contributions and their sums come with intervals, because every draw is decomposed. Sums over ages or causes are formed draw by draw (summary(by = )), so their intervals are not sums of intervals.
  • Cause-specific contributions are only as good as the coding of causes; trends in coding (dementia, ill-defined causes) move between causes, not in the total.
